# Proof

The answer is **yes**.

Let $(t_{ji})_{j \geq 1}$ be the matrix of $T$ in the standard basis $(e_i)$ of $\ell^2$, so $T(e_i) = \sum_{j=1}^\infty t_{ji}\, e_j$.

The Banach space $\ell^2(X)$ consists of sequences $(x_i)_{i \geq 1}$ in $X$ with $\sum_i \|x_i\|^2 < \infty$, normed by $\|(x_i)\| = \bigl(\sum_i \|x_i\|^2\bigr)^{1/2}$. The algebraic tensor product $\ell^2 \otimes_{\mathrm{alg}} X$ — finite sums $u = \sum_{i=1}^N e_i \otimes x_i$ — is dense in $\ell^2(X)$, identified with finitely supported sequences.

**Action of $T \otimes \mathrm{Id}_X$.** For $u = \sum_{i=1}^N e_i \otimes x_i$,
$$(T \otimes \mathrm{Id}_X)(u) = \sum_{i=1}^N T(e_i) \otimes x_i = \sum_{j=1}^\infty e_j \otimes \Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^N t_{ji}\, x_i\Bigr),$$
with norm
$$\|(T \otimes \mathrm{Id}_X)(u)\|^2 = \sum_{j=1}^\infty \Bigl\|\sum_{i=1}^N t_{ji}\, x_i\Bigr\|^2.$$
This is finite: by Cauchy–Schwarz and $\|T(e_i)\| \leq \|T\|$,
$$\sum_j \Bigl\|\sum_{i=1}^N t_{ji}\, x_i\Bigr\|^2 \leq N\sum_{i=1}^N \|x_i\|^2 \sum_j |t_{ji}|^2 = N\sum_{i=1}^N \|x_i\|^2\, \|T(e_i)\|^2 \leq N\|T\|^2 \|u\|^2 < \infty.$$
So $T \otimes \mathrm{Id}_X$ is a well-defined linear map from $\ell^2 \otimes_{\mathrm{alg}} X$ into $\ell^2(X)$.

**Using unboundedness.** By hypothesis, $T \otimes \mathrm{Id}_X$ is **not bounded** on $(\ell^2 \otimes_{\mathrm{alg}} X,\, \|\cdot\|_{\ell^2(X)})$. Hence for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ there exists a nonzero finite sum
$$u_n = \sum_{i=1}^{N_n} e_i \otimes x_i^{(n)} \in \ell^2 \otimes_{\mathrm{alg}} X$$
such that
$$\|(T \otimes \mathrm{Id}_X)(u_n)\|_{\ell^2(X)} > n\,\|u_n\|_{\ell^2(X)}. \tag{$\ast$}$$

**Constructing $X_n$.** Set
$$X_n = \operatorname{span}\{x_1^{(n)}, \dots, x_{N_n}^{(n)}\} \subseteq X.$$
This is a finite-dimensional subspace of $X$. Since each $x_i^{(n)} \in X_n$, we have $u_n \in \ell^2(X_n)$. Moreover, each component $\sum_{i=1}^{N_n} t_{ji}\, x_i^{(n)}$ lies in $X_n$ (as $X_n$ is a linear subspace), so $(T \otimes \mathrm{Id}_{X_n})(u_n)$ is the same element of $\ell^2(X_n)$ as $(T \otimes \mathrm{Id}_X)(u_n)$ viewed in $\ell^2(X)$. Therefore
$$\|(T \otimes \mathrm{Id}_{X_n})(u_n)\|_{\ell^2(X_n)} = \|(T \otimes \mathrm{Id}_X)(u_n)\|_{\ell^2(X)} > n\,\|u_n\|_{\ell^2(X)} = n\,\|u_n\|_{\ell^2(X_n)},$$
where the last equality holds because $u_n \in \ell^2(X_n)$ and the $\ell^2(X_n)$-norm coincides with the $\ell^2(X)$-norm on this subspace.

It follows that
$$\|T \otimes \mathrm{Id}_{X_n}\|_{\ell^2(X_n) \to \ell^2(X_n)} \geq \frac{\|(T \otimes \mathrm{Id}_{X_n})(u_n)\|}{\|u_n\|} > n.$$

**Conclusion.** The sequence $(X_n)$ of finite-dimensional subspaces satisfies
$$\|T \otimes \mathrm{Id}_{X_n}\|_{\ell^2(X_n) \to \ell^2(X_n)} \xrightarrow[n \to +\infty]{} +\infty. \qquad \blacksquare$$

### PROOF COMPLETE
